title: Many-to-many, views and ALTER TABLE
summary: Junction tables, saved queries, and changing a schema that already holds data.

steps.title: Many-to-many needs a junction table
body: A show has many performers, and a performer appears in many shows. Neither table can hold the link: `shows.performer_id` allows one performer per show, and a list in a cell breaks 1NF.
The answer is a **junction table** with one row per pairing:
```sql
CREATE TABLE show_cast (
show_id      INTEGER NOT NULL REFERENCES shows(id),
performer_id INTEGER NOT NULL REFERENCES performers(id),
role         TEXT NOT NULL,                 -- facts about the pairing live here
PRIMARY KEY (show_id, performer_id)         -- each pairing once
Query it with two joins: shows → show_cast → performers.

steps.prompt: Which relationship needs a junction table?
options: Students and courses: a student takes many courses, a course has many students
Orders and customers: an order has one customer
Doctors and their mentor: each doctor has at most one
Tickets and shows: a ticket is for one show
steps.explain: The other three are one-to-many: a foreign key column on the 'many' side is enough.

solution: CREATE TABLE show_cast (
show_id INTEGER NOT NULL REFERENCES shows(id),
performer_id INTEGER NOT NULL REFERENCES performers(id),
role TEXT NOT NULL,
PRIMARY KEY (show_id, performer_id)

steps.title: Views: saved queries
body: A **view** is a named SELECT that you query like a table:
```sql
CREATE VIEW playbill AS
SELECT s.title, s.starts, p.name AS performer, c.role
FROM shows AS s
JOIN show_cast AS c ON c.show_id = s.id
JOIN performers AS p ON p.id = c.performer_id;
SELECT * FROM playbill WHERE performer = 'Iris Vale';
- A view stores **no data**: it runs its query each time, so it's always current.
- It hides complexity (the website team doesn't need to know about junction tables) and can hide columns (no fees, no emails).
- `DROP VIEW playbill;` removes it. Some databases also have *materialised* views that store the result and need refreshing.

steps.title: The playbill
prompt: Create a view **`playbill`** with columns **`title`**, **`performer`** and **`role`**: one row per performer per show.
Tables: `shows(id, title, starts)`, `performers(id, name)`, `show_cast(show_id, performer_id, role)`.
solution: CREATE VIEW playbill AS
SELECT s.title, p.name AS performer, c.role
FROM shows AS s
JOIN show_cast AS c ON c.show_id = s.id
JOIN performers AS p ON p.id = c.performer_id;

steps.title: ALTER TABLE
body: Schemas change while the data stays. `ALTER TABLE` edits a table in place:
```sql fragment
ALTER TABLE shows ADD COLUMN runtime_min INTEGER;              -- existing rows get NULL
ALTER TABLE shows ADD COLUMN status TEXT NOT NULL DEFAULT 'on sale';  -- NOT NULL needs a DEFAULT
ALTER TABLE shows RENAME COLUMN starts TO starts_at;
ALTER TABLE shows RENAME TO productions;
ALTER TABLE shows DROP COLUMN runtime_min;                     -- SQLite 3.35+

SQLite's ALTER is limited: it can't add a constraint to an existing column. The standard workaround is *create a new table, copy the rows, drop the old one, rename*. PostgreSQL and SQL Server can `ALTER TABLE ... ADD CONSTRAINT ...` directly.
On big tables in production, some ALTERs rewrite every row and lock the table. Check before running them at noon.

steps.prompt: Complete the statement: add a required `status` column whose existing rows become 'on sale'.
steps.code: ALTER TABLE shows __1__ COLUMN status TEXT NOT NULL __2__ 'on sale';

steps.title: Who's free?
prompt: Rehearsals clash if a performer is cast in two shows. Return each pair of **show titles** that share at least one performer, plus the shared **performer** name: **show1**, **show2** (show1's id smaller), **performer**.
Tables: `shows(id, title, starts)`, `performers(id, name)`, `show_cast(show_id, performer_id, role)`.
solution: SELECT s1.title AS show1, s2.title AS show2, p.name AS performer
FROM show_cast AS a
JOIN show_cast AS b ON b.performer_id = a.performer_id AND a.show_id < b.show_id
JOIN shows AS s1 ON s1.id = a.show_id
JOIN shows AS s2 ON s2.id = b.show_id
JOIN performers AS p ON p.id = a.performer_id;
